notes: \cpara{Introduces the post's one case: a woman the author talked with for a few hours, described from the author's side of the conversation. As with the panelist in ``Professing and Cheering'' (see the notes there), what follows reads her state of mind from her words and manner.}

\cfact{The Persian records are not silent. The name Marduka, for officials of the Persian court, appears in over thirty Persepolis texts, and Wikipedia's ``Book of Esther'' says one of them ``might be the model for the biblical Mordecai.'' The link to Marduk and Ishtar is a scholarly conjecture from the 1890s.}
\cpara{A claim about ``most'' intelligent religious people, with no evidence. The linked post, ``Pretending to be Wise,'' is about neutrality in general and does not mention religion.}

\cpara{States the thesis and names it ``belief in self-deception.'' The author claims only to understand it better, not to have discovered it. For the philosophers' earlier accounts of self-deception as a belief about one's own beliefs, see the notes on ``Belief in Belief.''}
\cpara{Her account: an atheist in high school, she decided to act as if she believed, and came to believe. This is the method Pascal recommended (see the notes on ``Doublethink'').}

\cpara{The evidence, hedged (``So far as I can tell''): her phrasing, her talk only of the benefits of belief, and her agreement that someone who just wanted the truth ``would not even invent God as a hypothesis.'' The last is the strongest of the three.}

\clogic{The phrasing is weak evidence. ``I believe in God'' is the ordinary form of a profession of faith. Merriam-Webster's sense of ``believe'' for religious belief, ``usually used with in,'' is ``to regard the existence of God or a deity as a fact.'' In Jewish prayer, the thirteen lines of \textsc{Ani Ma'amin}, which many recite after the morning service, each begin ``I believe with full faith.''}
\cpara{Restates the conclusion, with the hedge kept.}
\cpara{The second half of the diagnosis, hedged with ``I think'': she believes she has deceived herself.}

\cpara{Infers that believing you have deceived yourself brings ``much the same placebo effect'' as real belief. In ``Doublethink'' (2007) the author had written that you ``might even believe you were happy and self-deceived; but you would not in fact be happy and self-deceived.'' Read strictly, that sentence denies only that you would be both, so the two claims can be reconciled; the post does not do so.}
\clogic{Offered with ``I suppose'' and no evidence, either that belief in God benefits believers through their expectations or that believing you believe brings the same benefit.}
\cpara{Uses the placebo idea, hedged (``may explain''), to account for her defending ``I believe in God'' while showing no interest in whether God exists.}
